# Evaluation that controls adoption helps determine the change

> Supplement to the adoption-versus-measurement distinction in [the better-factory comparison](./a-better-factory-claim-compares-operative-states.md).

An evaluator who controls whether a proposed change enters use helps determine which system results. An evaluator who only assesses an already-adopted change does not, through that assessment alone, determine its adoption. The difference is what the judgment controls, not whether a person or a program makes it.

This matters when deciding whose contributions explain a system's improvement. A human approval required for adoption is part of the process that selected the revision. A later human assessment is not evidence of that same contribution to selection.

## The same activity can perform different roles

Consider an agent that proposes a new KB instruction. These are hypothetical cases, not reports of observed behavior.

**Approval before adoption.** The agent proposes the instruction, a maintainer examines test results, and the agent adopts it only after the maintainer approves. The maintainer's judgment helps select the instruction that enters use. An account of how this change was selected must include that judgment.

**Assessment after adoption.** The agent adopts the instruction under its existing rules. A week later, the maintainer examines the results and concludes that the instruction helped. This judgment assesses an existing change; it did not decide whether that instruction entered use.

Both cases involve reading results and forming a verdict. Only the first verdict controls the adoption being examined. The later assessment could still cause a future revision or a rollback. That would give it a causal role in a different transition.

## One episode can contain both roles

A maintainer might approve a proposed instruction and later assess its effects in use. The episode then contains both selection and assessment. Calling the whole episode an evaluation does not identify which judgment did which work.

The account must name the change and the decision being examined. Whether approval was required for that adoption is a fact about the process. A different description cannot turn required approval into assessment after adoption.

Adoption here means entering a live behavioral path on which later operation depends, as distinguished by [operative change](./definitions/operative-change.md). A favorable assessment of a proposal that is never adopted does not establish an improvement of the deployed system.

## Scope

- This distinction concerns the causal role of a particular judgment. It does not establish that a later evaluator had no other influence on the system.
- Participation in selection does not by itself determine whether the evaluator counts as part of the learner. That depends on the declared system boundary. An externally supplied selection judgment must still be acknowledged as a contribution.
- Approval does not establish quality. An evaluator can select a harmful revision, just as a later assessment can misjudge its effects. A test available to the proposing system can be optimized without improving the capability it is meant to assess; human approval does not remove the need to justify the assessment.

## Open Questions

- How should an improvement claim report externally supplied adoption judgments when the evaluator is outside its declared learner boundary?

# Revise an article or note

Make the artifact serve the operator's stated purpose without changing what it
claims, by assessing first and then running only the passes the assessment
recommends. This is a planning-containing procedure. When the purpose, scope
and pass are already fixed, use the fixed-plan route in the
[simplification-pass guide](./README.md#fixed-plan-execution-the-simple-baseline)
instead of assessing again.

## Prerequisites

- A purpose in one line: who the reader is and what they should notice or be
  able to do. If the operator named only the artifact, propose the purpose
  at the top of the assessment and proceed under it; the operator corrects
  it if it is wrong.
- The artifact's claims are settled. A claim in dispute goes to the operator
  as a question, not into a pass.

## Steps

1. **Assess before editing.** Read the whole artifact. Report a ranked list
   of changes, highest value against the purpose first, each with its cost
   in one phrase and the pass from this directory that would make it. Name
   the sentence a hostile reviewer would attack first. Say what reads well
   in one sentence. Recommend only passes whose value against the purpose
   is clear; an item you would not defend is not recommended. Do not edit.

   If the highest-value change is a rewrite or a restructuring of the
   argument, report that and stop. The passes work on text, and text a
   rewrite will replace is not worth a pass; recommend passes only over the
   parts the assessment expects to survive.

   When the assessment finds that a claim itself is wrong or unsupported,
   the passes cannot fix it: they do not change claims. Set the plan's
   `stop`, name the claim, and name the rewrite route:
   `commonplace-review run rewrite NOTE --commission FILE`, with the
   commission prepared with `cp-skill-write-multistage`.

   Two things the passes cannot own belong in the assessment too. For each
   candidate overclaim, propose whether the sentence is support (may be
   narrowed) or divergence (must be kept); the divergence items become the
   packets' `Must keep:` line unless the operator objects. And list
   qualifications that have gone stale against the body: a scope bullet
   qualifying words the body no longer uses, a table cell filed under the
   wrong row, a cross-note ordinal pointing at the wrong list. These are
   claim questions for the operator, applied as their own commits after
   approval, not passes.

   Review findings may come with the artifact. Each is a stored review
   result with outcome `warn` or `fail`, and each names its criterion and
   the depth that criterion declares. Read them with the artifact. By
   default, a finding at depth *n* points at the pass at depth *n*. A
   finding whose criterion is named in a pass's `responds-to` may instead
   become a plan entry for that pass, with the result file as the entry's
   `finding`. That entry takes the depth of the finding's criterion in the
   order. [Fix a finding by a named strategy](../fix-warnings/fix-strategy-taxonomy.md)
   is such a pass: it changes only the passage the finding names. Recommend
   the change a finding points at only when its value against the purpose
   is clear. List the findings you do not act on once, each with its reason.

   The operator's decisions on findings of the artifact may come as
   `earlier-decisions`: findings the operator rejected or deferred at a
   triage, each with the operator's reason. Plan no fix for a finding the
   operator rejected unless the text changed in a way that answers the
   operator's reason; say so when you plan one. Plan no fix for a deferred finding unless its
   `revisit` condition is met.

   Depth 1 review reports may come with the artifact as well: critique,
   composition friction and premise decomposition. If one of them proposes
   changing what the artifact is (a split, a merge, a different claim or a
   rejection), set the plan's `stop` and list no passes. The stop names the
   proposal and the repository path of the report it comes from. The run
   then ends with nothing edited, and the operator decides the proposal.
   When the proposal is to move a full argument into a separate file, the
   stop may recommend [split out a treatment](./split-out-a-treatment.md);
   no procedure runs it.

   The [role report](../role-in-the-kb-gate.md) may come as well. It states
   the artifact's role in the KB from the passages that link to it: what
   each dependent needs from it, what it duplicates, and which
   recommendations in linking sources it has not taken up. It does not
   judge whether a claim is good theory: do not plan to cut content
   because no dependent uses it. Read it before
   you stop on a depth 1 proposal or plan around one. Check whether the
   proposal's cause may be a term or claim that dependents rely on: a
   contradiction inside the artifact can come from a term a dependent
   uses in another sense. When the proposed change, or a pass you would
   plan, changes a claim or term that dependents rely on, set `stop` and
   name those dependents in it, with the role report's run directory: the
   passes edit only the artifact, so the operator must decide the
   dependents' change too.

2. **Dispatch each recommended pass as a packet.** Proceed without waiting;
   the report gives the operator the chance to interrupt. Run passes one at a time,
   since they share one write scope. Order them by depth, not by the
   assessment's ranking: a pass whose edits a later pass would rewrite runs
   after it. The order that has held is split-out-a-treatment,
   narrow-overclaims, abstractions, readability-and-flow, plain-wording,
   opening-and-title. Abstractions runs before the structural moves although
   it is a wording pass, because one name per thing is what makes a
   duplicated caveat or two paragraphs on one subject visible; the opening
   runs last because the TL;DR restates a body the earlier passes have
   settled. Make the plain-wording list after the structural moves land; a
   list made against the earlier text names passages that have moved or
   gone. Each pass file carries an `effort`
   field: `simple` passes run in a fresh worker on a cheaper model or lower
   effort; `judgment` passes run on the session model, in the current
   context or a fresh worker. Use a fresh worker when the pass benefits from
   not having seen the conversation, as the plain-wording and
   readability passes do; run narrow-overclaims in the parent context, where
   the conversation is the evidence. Apply one-word swaps and two-sentence
   narrowings in the parent context rather than as packets. Small scoped
   edits from different passes may share one packet when its scope is
   enumerated. The packet is:

   ```
   Purpose: {the operator's one line}
   Artifact: {path}
   Pass: {absolute path of {pass}.md in this instruction's directory}
   Must keep: {what this run keeps beyond the write brief's Must keep; a pass may not narrow it}
   Write scope: {the artifact only | none, return proposals}
   Return: the pass's report, plus items noticed but not applied, nothing committed
   ```

   The worker chooses means within the pass. It does not widen the write
   scope, add claims, or remove evidence.

3. **Integrate.** After each pass read the diff, and read every replaced
   phrase in its full sentence, not in the diff summary; a literal
   replacement can supply a referent the original left implicit and supply
   the wrong one. List each mapping, contrast, example, price, or link the
   diff removed and check that the pass report accounts for it; restore what
   it does not, in the classes [audit-a-prior-pass](./audit-a-prior-pass.md)
   uses. A pass that narrows or tightens a sentence tends to take its
   neighbours with it. Run `commonplace-validate` on the artifact, and commit the
   pass alone with a body saying what it was meant to make true. If the operator reverts part of a pass, record the
   threshold they applied in the pass file or a memory, so the next run
   starts from it.

4. **Stop when the recommended passes are done.** Report what each pass
   changed. Items you assessed but did not recommend, and the not-applied
   items the workers returned, are listed once, not run.

## Run it as a workflow

`commonplace-review run revise ARTIFACT --assess --purpose TEXT [--must-keep CLAIM ...]`
runs these steps with headless workers, which never write the checkout. This
is the quick procedure. The assessment also receives the artifact's fresh
stored review results with outcome `warn` or `fail`, when any exist; the
command launches no review. Results with only INFO-level findings are not
given. A finding the operator rejected at a triage of the same result is
removed, and the operator's rejected and deferred findings of the artifact
come as `earlier-decisions`. The focused procedure makes no assessment: `--pass NAME` runs a
one-entry plan for that pass, and `--finding RESULT` runs a one-entry plan
that fixes that review result of the artifact. The triage, `--triage`, makes
no assessment either: it stops with one answers file per fresh `warn` or
`fail` result, the operator decides each finding with
[decide items](../decide-items.md), and the plan fixes the approved findings
only, one entry per result with an approved finding. The full procedure, `--full`,
first runs every review operation that declares a `depth` on the artifact,
through the same route as `commonplace-review run gates`. Its results go to
the shared store, and fresh results are reused. The compression synthesis
then runs on the compression checks' results, and the role report on the
artifact's inbound contexts; neither publishes a result. The assessment
receives the fresh `warn` and `fail` results, the depth 1 reports, the
synthesis report and the role report. A review that ends without a result stops the run before the
assessment. The full procedure does not review the edited text. Its
run directory is derived from the artifact's path and the hash of its text.
It stops with a proposal wherever this procedure waits for the operator.
Repeating alone never approves the proposal or starts its dependent work.
A repeat reuses the recorded `--purpose`, `--must-keep` and profiles unless you
give them again. Each approval stop prints a JSON report whose `waiting-for` gives
what to do, the file, proposal key, `approve-command` and command to repeat.
Assessment, planning and settled intermediate passes are preauthorized;
never wait for routine plan approval. Each stop's file is a pending
[answers](../../types/answers.md) file: record the operator's decision on its
items before the `approve-command`, then repeat the workflow command.
Approval captures that text; later edits require approval again and are
listed under `unapproved-edits`. Changed proposal inputs require fresh approval. An agent
may approve only on the operator's stated word for that specific proposal;
it must not infer approval from a request to retry. This instruction and the
pass files own judgment; worker prompts name inputs, not additional criteria.

1. Step 1 runs as one assessment ask, on the profile for `judgment`. The run
   retains `assessment.md` and `plan.yaml` under the run directory's
   `artifact/` for inspection and proceeds with the validated plan.
   `--plan FILE` supplies an explicit input or override without assessment
   or approval, including replacement of a stopped plan. The plan holds
   `purpose`, `must-keep`, `passes` in run order (each a `pass` name, an
   optional `scope` and, for a pass that declares `responds-to`, the
   `finding` it fixes) and `stop`. A plan with `stop` set ends the run without
   editing the artifact. To run passes instead, supply a replacement with
   `stop` cleared and the desired passes through `--plan`; editing the
   retained `artifact/plan.yaml` alone is not an override.
   A stopped plan also leaves `artifact/stop-answers.md`, an
   [answers](../../types/answers.md) file with one item for the plan. The
   run does not wait for it; its report names it under `stop-answers`.
   Record the operator's decision on the proposal there: `approved` to act
   on it as made, or `rejected` or `deferred` with the operator's reason.
   When the work that followed is done, add `resolution` (what was done,
   when it differs from or goes beyond the proposal) and `refs` (commit
   hashes, paths, a workshop directory) to the item. Run the reported
   approval command each time the file changes, so that
   `commonplace-review decisions` lists the current text.
   The command rejects a plan that names an unknown pass, misses a field,
   has a field it does not know,
   names a `finding` that is not a review result of the artifact, or breaks
   the depth order the pass files and the findings' criteria declare. A replacement supplied
   with `--plan` reuses calls whose inputs did not change and reruns the others.
2. Step 2 runs each listed pass as one run of the edit route, the same one
   `commonplace-review run edit` uses, on the profile from
   `instructions/review-profiles.yaml` that its `effort` selects. Code checks
   the edit result and the revised text (title, type, brief declaration and
   H1 kept; no new validation failure; link targets and quoted spans kept),
   and the next pass works on that text. Each run's result and candidate are
   retained under `artifact/edits/`. Every pass must end
   `applied`, `no-change` or `skipped` before the final text is published.
   After a `problem` pass the run publishes nothing more, and
   `not-published` names the run file holding the proposed text.
   The workflow does not commit.
3. A pass whose `decision` is `per-item` (plain-wording, abstractions) first
   returns proposals, and stops with the pending answers file
   `artifact/<pass>-answers-<key>.md`: one item per proposal, holding its
   `quote`, `change` and `reason`, every item `pending`. In a session, follow
   [decide items](../decide-items.md): the agent presents each item in
   context, asks, and records the operator's answer as `approved`,
   `rejected` with a reason, or `deferred` with a reason and a revisit
   condition. Run the stop's approval command, then repeat; the same
   operation runs again with the answers file as its `answers` input and
   applies only the `approved` items. Code refuses a candidate that changed
   the passage of an item that is not approved. Answers the validator
   refuses stop the run again naming the problem: correct the file and
   approve it again. Answers that approve no item end the pass as
   `no-change`. Proposals made again for another text get a new file and
   stop again. Decisions carry over between runs on the same note. When a
   run starts, code collects the operator's decided items from the earlier
   runs on the note and keeps them in the run as `earlier-decisions.json`.
   The pass receives them as its `earlier-decisions` input. A proposal with
   the same `quote` and `change` as an item the operator already decided
   starts decided as before, with `carried-from` naming the earlier answers
   file. The run still stops, and the operator may change such an item.
   Every other proposal is asked as usual. These are temporary procedure-development points for
   unsettled selection rules. The run retains the answers with each
   rejection's and deferral's reason in the operator's words. Use them to revise
   selection rules and checks, then evaluate those changes on retained and
   fresh examples before seeking separate authorization to remove a
   selection stop. This requires no new automatic learning infrastructure;
   fewer proposals alone do not establish reliability.
4. Narrow-overclaims runs only when the plan's `must-keep` list is not empty.
   Split-out-a-treatment does not run. Both are reported as skipped, left
   for this procedure in a conversation.
5. The command publishes a changed text to the artifact without a stop:
   before it waits at a per-item stop, what the earlier passes applied, and
   at the end of the plan, the final text. Approved items are published when
   applied, with no second approval. It writes only while the artifact holds
   the text the run last knew and the captured brief is unchanged. Each
   publication is kept under `artifact/publications/` with its diff and
   listed in the report's `publications`. Nothing is committed. After a run
   publishes, follow [approve a text](../approve-a-text.md): tell the
   operator what was published, with the path of the note and of the diff;
   `git diff` shows the change, and the operator reverses it with git.
   A final text that adds a validation warning the artifact does not have
   stops at `artifact/publication-answers.md` instead. Follow
   [approve a text](../approve-a-text.md): inspect `artifact/final.md` and
   `artifact/final.diff`, record the operator's decision on the answers
   file's one item, which names the candidate's hash, then run the report's
   `commonplace-review approve RUN FILE --key KEY` command and repeat.
   Repeating never approves. Do not edit the candidate to revise the text:
   supply `--plan`, change workflow inputs, or start a new run.
6. An artifact edited between invocations has another hash, so the command
   opens a new run. A run that published before a per-item stop is the
   exception: the command finds it by the text it published. Choose `--assess` again to commission planning,
   `--triage` to decide the findings, or `--plan FILE` to execute fixed work. A bare command does not choose a mode. An artifact changed during a run, or by anyone else after the run published, is a conflict: nothing
   is written, and the report names the run file holding the proposed text.

Step 3 stays with the operator: each pass's report and the text it left are
under `artifact/reports/` and `artifact/texts/`; read each diff after the
run publishes. If a report does not account for an edit, revise through workflow
inputs or `--plan`, not by editing the generated candidate, or reverse the
publication with git. Commit only after the operator has seen the
published diff. Use this procedure in a
conversation instead when the passes are chosen as the conversation goes,
when a pass needs the conversation as evidence, or when each pass should be
integrated and committed before the next one runs.

## Headless write briefs

When the artifact declares a [write brief](../../types/write-brief.md), the assessment and every pass
(including candidate-list and apply workers) receive its captured text as
`brief`. Pass workers receive [execute a revision pass](./execute-a-revision-pass.md)
as `execution`, not this planning procedure. That execution instruction carries
the pass bounds and brief constraints without commissioning assessment or dispatch.

Treat the supplied brief as binding retained intent. It is the one lasting
statement of what the artifact must keep and exclude. Keep its Must keep,
Must exclude and Reserved decisions in both the plan and the edited text.
Do not amend the brief or remove or change the artifact's `brief:` field.

The plan starts from the brief. Its `must-keep` lists only what this run adds
to the brief's Must keep: the operator's must-keep items and the claims the
assessment marks as divergence. Do not restate the brief's items there; every
pass receives the brief. Never plan a pass that conflicts with the brief.
When the purpose or the operator's must-keep items conflict with the brief,
set the plan's `stop`, list no passes, and name the brief item and the
conflicting text.

A pass worker that finds the purpose, the must-keep list, the validated plan,
an approved candidate list or its instruction in conflict with the brief
reports the conflict through the worker-problem output and stops. Selection
or publication approval does not authorise amending the brief. The operator
must resolve the commission change outside this workflow before continuing.

Use the captured input, not a reread of the live brief. A brief change between
invocations invalidates affected calls and dependent approvals; a change during an
invocation blocks publication. A missing or invalid declared brief stops the
run before workers launch. Supplying it does not mechanically verify that
an edit respects its meaning; the worker must identify conflicts.

## Budget

- The assessment is one full read. Each pass is one more. Do not re-read
  linked notes unless a pass names them.
- A worker gets the artifact path and the packet, never the conversation.
- Propose-only work (the assessment, the plain-wording list, title
  proposals) may run in parallel; edits to the artifact run in sequence.
- Stop when the recommended passes are done. An item not recommended costs
  nothing; recommending a pass of unclear value costs a read and a diff.

## Verify

- Every applied change traces to a recommended pass.
- Every passage a diff weakened is accounted for by that pass's report.
- No claim, evidence, or qualification changed unless the operator asked.
- Conversational execution validates and commits each integrated pass. The
  headless workflow instead retains per-pass reports and checked texts, and
  writes the artifact only through its recorded publications, without
  committing.
- Operator reverts have been recorded as thresholds.

# Review

## Summary

The core vocabulary works for a first-time reader. The two worked cases define "approval before adoption" and "assessment after adoption" through what the evaluator controls. "Adoption" receives an inline gloss, "entering a live behavioral path on which later operation depends", next to its link to the operative-change definition, so the link is not doing the defining.

The gap is in the Scope section. "The learner" and its "declared system boundary" import a framework concept from elsewhere in the KB without saying what it is. This is the one place where the reader would have to know KB context to follow the sentence. The supplement pointer's "better-factory comparison" is opaque but has little effect on comprehension.

# Review

The title is a proposition, but its predicate nearly follows from its subject. "Controls adoption" already means the judgment decides whether a change enters use. So "helps determine the change" adds little that a knowledgeable reader could dispute.

The note's live claim is in the contrast and its consequence. Required approval before adoption is part of the selection that explains a system's improvement. Assessment after adoption is not, and calling both "evaluation" does not erase the difference. Someone who treats all evaluation as external measurement of a self-improving system could reasonably contest that claim. The title should state it.

# Review

The main claim is that a judgment helps determine a change when it controls whether the change enters use. Assessment after adoption does not, through that assessment alone, contribute to selecting the change. What matters is the judgment's causal role, not whether a person or program makes it.

Most of the side material supports that claim in its current place:

- The two hypothetical cases are the note's central contrast.
- The remark that a later assessment could cause a future rollback limits the claim to the transition under examination.
- "One episode can contain both roles" blocks the redescription move named in the description.
- The definition of adoption, with its link to operative change, fixes the term the claim depends on.
- The first two Scope bullets are boundary conditions. The second also motivates the single open question.
- The first two sentences of the third bullet ("Approval does not establish quality…") are also a boundary condition. They stop readers from treating selection as endorsement.

The final sentence of that bullet is the one branch that needs action. It introduces test optimization by the proposing system. That is a different failure mechanism, with its own evidence requirements, and the note neither defends it nor needs it. Here it widens the attack surface and shifts the reader's attention from causal role to evaluation validity. Removing it leaves the boundary condition intact.

# Review

## Summary

The note sets out a two-way distinction: judgment that controls whether a change enters use, and assessment of a change that is already adopted. It defines control by whether approval was required for adoption. I tested five boundary cases against that criterion.

- **Simplest case: required approval that is granted.** It maps cleanly to control.
- **Post-adoption assessment that triggers a rollback.** The note explicitly treats this as a causal role in a different transition.
- **One evaluator who approves and later assesses.** The section on one episode containing both roles handles this.
- **Advisory pre-adoption review.** This case falls between the two roles. The judgment comes before adoption and can influence it, but it is not required. The note's binary does not cover it, and its scope caveat covers only later evaluators. This is the warning finding.
- **Criteria authored in advance and applied by a program.** This case can be mapped, but only with difficulty.

The taxonomy is short and fits its argumentative role. Adding a third category may not be the right fix. The note could instead say that judgments which are not required but come before adoption fall outside its claim.

# Friction check: Evaluation that controls adoption helps determine the change

**Central claim (one sentence):** A judgment contributes to which system revision results when it controls whether that revision is adopted, and an assessment of an already-adopted change does not make that contribution to its adoption, regardless of who or what makes the judgment.

## Filter
**Filter:** SURVIVES

The note wants three things at once: the distinction is role-based rather than agent-based, one episode can contain both roles, and redescription cannot move a judgment between roles. These coexist. Roles attach to particular judgments relative to a named transition, so one maintainer can approve and later assess, and the process facts fix which judgment controlled adoption. The concession that later assessment may cause a different transition (rollback or future revision) keeps the claim scoped to one transition rather than splitting it.

## Thinnest joints

The weakest joint is the step from "approval was required" to "approval helped select". The central claim is stated in terms of control, but every worked inference uses requirement. These come apart exactly in the rubber-stamp case, and the note's description-invariance argument depends on the stronger notion it never states. The second joint is related: even granting control, the note treats selection as contributing to improvement. Its own Scope disclaimer ("Approval does not establish quality") weakens that link. The Goodhart sentence and the acknowledgement obligation are thinner as inferences than as claims. Each reads plausibly, but the note does not supply the connecting premise. The unadopted-proposal joint holds because the linked definition carries it.

## For the human
Look first at whether "controls adoption" needs a counterfactual condition (the evaluator could and sometimes would refuse) so that required-but-nondiscriminating approval is not counted as selection.

# Critique: Evaluation that controls adoption helps determine the change

**Note:** kb/theory/evaluation-that-controls-adoption-helps-determine-the-change.md
**Central commitment:** An evaluator's judgment contributes to selecting a system revision exactly when the judgment controls whether the change enters use; assessment after adoption does not make that contribution, and this role is fixed by the process, not by how the episode is described.
**Critique mode:** claim
**Attack outcome:** partially lands

## Strongest case against it

The opponent holds an interventionist, difference-making view of causation, as in Woodward's account or the counterfactual tradition. On that view, a judgment helps determine which system results when changing the judgment would have changed the resulting system. The note's criterion is different. It uses process position: whether the judgment's approval was required and whether it came before or after entry into use. The opponent argues that process position and difference-making come apart in both directions.

1. **Required but idle.** Suppose a maintainer must approve every proposed instruction but in practice approves whatever passes the agent's own tests. The approval is required, so the note says the maintainer "helps select the instruction that enters use". Counterfactually, nothing would change if the maintainer were replaced by an automatic pass. The note also says "Whether approval was required for that adoption is a fact about the process". The opponent answers that it is the wrong fact. A formal gate is a place where selection could happen. It does not show that selection happened.

2. **After adoption but selective.** Suppose the agent adopts instructions under its own rules, and a maintainer reviews them a week later and rolls back the ones judged unhelpful. If the improvement claim compares the predecessor with the operative state at a measurement boundary, the maintainer's judgments decide which instructions are in that state. The linked better-factory note explicitly allows this form: "the successor can instead be the operative state at a named measurement boundary". So does the operative-change definition: "a change later rolled back was operative while it held". The note calls rollback "a causal role in a different transition". The opponent says this classification depends on choosing to examine entry into use rather than the state at the boundary. That choice is descriptive, which is the kind of choice the note says cannot change the attribution.

3. **Anticipation.** A proposer that knows a later assessment will happen can write changes to survive it. The later assessor then shapes which changes are proposed and adopted without making any judgment before adoption.

Together, these cases say that the before/after distinction tracks formal authority and not causal contribution to selection. Those are the two things the note says it separates.

## How the note engages it

**Partially engaged.**

- On anticipation, the note hedges in its opening: "through that assessment alone". Its Scope section also says the distinction "does not establish that a later evaluator had no other influence on the system." This answers objection 3 well enough, because the claim is about the role of one judgment, not about the evaluator's total effect. The mechanism, however, is not named.
- On rollback, the note concedes that later assessment can cause a rollback and assigns it to "a different transition". It also requires that "The account must name the change and the decision being examined." This is the right lever. However, the note does not say that the choice of transition is part of the declared comparison, or that under a boundary-defined successor (which its parent note allows) keep-or-rollback judgment is selection for the very transition being examined. As written, the worked "Assessment after adoption" case suggests that later assessment never selects for the improvement claim. That holds only when the examined transition is entry into use.
- On required-but-idle approval, the note does not engage. The Scope bullet "Approval does not establish quality" is about whether the selected revision is good, not whether the approval did any selecting. The claim "the difference is what the judgment controls" equates control with the authority to block, without asking whether that authority was exercised in any way sensitive to the candidate.

The note's core point survives: a judgment that comes after a change is in use cannot have been what let that change in, and relabelling an episode cannot erase a judgment that was required. The objection succeeds against the stronger reading. The note's verbs ("helps determine which system results", "helps select") claim causal contribution, and it supports them only with formal process position.

## Constructive findings

- Make the causal claim conditional on sensitivity. A required approval helps select a revision when the judgment could have rejected that candidate, or when the proposer filtered candidates against it. Otherwise, call it adoption authority and stop there. An unexercised gate is still worth recording, because it shows where selection could be audited, but it is not evidence of a selective contribution.
- Tie the "different transition" move to the declared comparison. State that which transition is examined, whether entry into use or the operative state at a measurement boundary, is fixed when the comparison is declared, as the parent note requires for its other parameters. Under a boundary-defined successor, a post-adoption assessment with rollback authority counts as selection. This keeps the note's anti-redescription principle: what is fixed in advance is the transition, and redescription afterwards cannot move the judgment.
- Name anticipation as a separate path. Say that a later assessor's influence on what is proposed is real causal influence, and that it is outside this distinction because the distinction classifies a judgment's role, not an evaluator's total effect.

## Secondary objections (optional)

- The worked "Assessment after adoption" case puts the selective work into "its existing rules". Those rules were themselves adopted, possibly with the same maintainer's approval. The note could say that an earlier adoption judgment over the adoption rule is a selection contribution one level up. Otherwise, a reader may conclude that the maintainer had no role in selection at all.
- The open question about external adoption judgments outside the learner boundary overlaps with the Scope bullet that already requires such a judgment to "be acknowledged as a contribution". The open part is narrower than stated: how to report the judgment, not whether to report it.

**Central commitment (one sentence):** A judgment that controls whether a proposed change enters use is part of the process that selects the resulting system, whereas a judgment that only assesses an already-adopted change is not part of that change's selection; which role a judgment plays is a process fact fixed by what it controls, not by who makes it or how the episode is described.

## Premises and counterexamples

The commitment has two halves and one invariance clause, and each consumes different premises.

The positive half ("controls adoption → helps determine the change") rests on treating gating control as a selection contribution. This is the most consequential node. A gate can be required and still make no counterfactual difference, as in a rubber stamp. The note needs a counterfactual or anticipatory qualification to make "control" carry the weight it puts on it.

The negative half ("assessment after adoption does not determine that adoption") is nearly definitional. It rests on individuating transitions, which the note does explicitly. Staged rollouts, rollbacks and anticipated evaluation all sort correctly under the note's own requirement to name the change and the decision. Those premises hold.

The invariance clause ("a different description cannot turn required approval into assessment") rests on "required" being a determinate fact. It becomes one only if the term is read counterfactually, not as the stated rule.

One premise is unstated. The note's motivating use is explaining "whose contributions explain a system's improvement". That use assumes selection lives in per-change judgments. The note's own second case adopts the change under "existing rules", whose authors are selectors the two-role partition does not name.

The approval-does-not-establish-quality and outside-the-learner points are scope concessions, not premises the commitment consumes, so they are not decomposed.

## For the human

Look first at the gate premise: decide whether "controls adoption" means a formal requirement or a verdict that could have gone otherwise, because a rubber-stamp approval satisfies the first and contributes nothing under the second.
